label: World as of 22 Oct 2026
lead: The world starts from real news: Suez traffic is returning after years of detours, Hormuz is closed, and on 10 November Beijing decides on export controls.

briefing.short: More than half of pre-crisis traffic is back in the Suez Canal. A full return is expected in Q1 2027, but the Red Sea is not fully safe yet.
briefing.title: Suez is coming back, cautiously
briefing.body: In the first two weeks of October an average of 753,000 TEU a week transited the Suez Canal, for the first time more than half the level before the Red Sea crisis. The consultancy Linerlytica expects a full return in Q1 2027. On 7 October, however, the CUL Klang, a Chinese-operated container ship, reported a security incident in the southern Red Sea.

briefing.short: The strait has been closed to shipping since March and Brent is around $102. Talks on reopening it go on.
briefing.title: Hormuz closed, oil at $100
briefing.body: The Strait of Hormuz has remained practically closed to shipping since March. On 5 October Brent cost about $102.6, 57% more than a year earlier. Governments are still negotiating a reopening, which could come within a week of a deal.

briefing.short: Spot Asia → North Europe is $3,726/FEU and has been falling since July, but it is still expensive.
briefing.title: Freight has eased since July, but is still expensive
briefing.body: According to Xeneta, the spot rate from the Far East to North Europe was $3,726/FEU on 1 October (−2.1% week on week), and $4,105 to the Mediterranean. The peak after the Hormuz crisis has passed, but freight is expected to stay high until the end of the year.

briefing.short: China promises easier licences for rare earths and magnets, and fewer hybrid cars for Europe. The next round is due by January.
briefing.title: EU and China: first agreements
briefing.body: On 9 October the Commission and China agreed to ease export licensing for rare earths and magnets further, through a “green channel”, and reached a shared understanding to halve China’s exports of hybrid cars to the EU. Talks on price undertakings for Chinese electric cars go on. Šefčovič calls it a first step; ministers meet again by January 2027.

briefing.short: The pause on export controls for rare earths and batteries runs out. Three scenarios.
briefing.title: Pause on Chinese export controls ends on 10 November
briefing.body: A year ago Beijing suspended its expanded export controls on rare earths and some lithium-battery items until 10 Nov 2026. Analysts see three scenarios: an extension, a selective return of licensing, or a full return of the controls.

briefing.short: A fifth of new cars sold in the EU this year are electric, up from 16% a year ago.
briefing.title: Electric cars pass a fifth of new sales
briefing.body: From January to August 2026, 21.7% of the new cars registered in the EU were battery-electric, against 15.8% a year earlier (ACEA). In August alone 196,486 were sold, 62.7% more than in August 2025; Germany is up 53% on the year and France 74%. Every one of them comes out of warranty a few years from now.

briefing.short: New EU rules: carmakers may check a workshop's tools, but not lock it out. Battery repair data is now included.
briefing.title: Workshops get the data to fix electric cars
briefing.body: Since 23 June, Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/699 sets what carmakers may demand before an independent workshop reads or changes a car's data: certificates for the tool and the workshop, nothing more. The repair information they must share now covers battery diagnostics and battery repair, and more of it must be available through an online interface.

briefing.short: LFP cells from China at $57/kWh in September. Lithium fell sharply in mid-September.
briefing.title: Battery cells get cheaper again
briefing.body: Standard LFP prismatic cells from China cost $57.37/kWh in September, 5.1% less than in August, and NCM cells fell 6.8% over the quarter (Benchmark). Lithium prices dropped sharply on 16 September. Cheaper cells mean cheaper battery modules: the stock you hold is worth a little less.

briefing.short: Memory chips are getting pricier, and so are electronics and power electronics for cars. The shortage may last until 2028.
briefing.title: Memory crunch hits electronics
briefing.body: DRAM and NAND prices have been rising for months, and in Q2 some components more than doubled in price. Electronics, including the control boards in inverters and onboard chargers, are getting more expensive, and the shortage may last until 2028.

briefing.short: ver.di wants an 8.2% raise. An indefinite strike in Hamburg and Bremerhaven is possible.
briefing.title: Pay dispute at German ports
briefing.body: In August ver.di held 24-hour warning strikes at six ports, including Hamburg and Bremerhaven. The union wants an 8.2% raise, while employers offered 5.1% over 19 months. The ballot on an indefinite strike closed on 1 October.

briefing.short: 85–90% of trains from China enter the EU at Małaszewicze. The border sometimes closes.
briefing.title: China–EU rail: everything goes through Małaszewicze
briefing.body: 85–90% of trains from China enter the EU through Małaszewicze. In September 2025 Poland closed its border with Belarus for almost two weeks, and this traffic came to a halt.

briefing.short: Only 36–39% of container ships arrive on time. Expect delays at ports.
briefing.title: Ships rarely arrive on time
briefing.body: From March to June only 36–39% of container ships called at ports on schedule, with an average delay of about 3.6 days. In the game this shows up as random delays at destination ports.

preview.title: In a week: Beijing decides on export controls
preview.body: The pause on export controls runs out on 10 November. After the 9 October agreements Brussels hopes for an extension, but analysts do not rule out a return of licensing for magnets and batteries. Your battery modules, heat pumps and drive units come mainly from China.

choices.label: Build 4 weeks of stock
choices.desc: Extra orders for battery modules and thermal parts in China, expedited (+3% on price).

choices.label: Fast-track Hanbit (Korea)
choices.desc: Urgent audit: €220k and 12 days instead of 28. Hanbit makes battery modules and heat pumps.

choices.label: Wait for the decision
choices.desc: No extra cost. You stick with the current plan.

outcomes.title: Beijing extends the pause by a year
outcomes.body: China’s Ministry of Commerce extends the suspension of the controls until November 2027. The market breathes a sigh of relief.

outcomes.title: Licences return for magnets and batteries
outcomes.body: China brings back export licences for permanent magnets and some batteries. Clearance takes weeks, and prices rise across the industry.

outcomes.title: Chinese export controls return in full
outcomes.body: Beijing brings back every measure from October 2025. Exports of batteries and of compressors with magnets need licences, and factories cut production for export.

outcomes.title: Strait of Hormuz reopens
outcomes.body: A deal is reached and tankers start leaving the Persian Gulf. Oil gets cheaper and carriers cut their bunker surcharges.

outcomes.title: Hormuz stays shut
outcomes.body: Talks stall and tanker traffic stays blocked. Brent goes up, and bunker surcharges with it.

events.title: The great return to Suez
events.body: The largest alliances restore full schedules through the Red Sea. Asia–Europe voyages get about 10 days shorter, and the freed-up fleet pushes rates down.

events.title: Indefinite strike at German ports
events.body: ver.di calls an indefinite strike in Hamburg, Bremerhaven and Wilhelmshaven. Ships wait at anchor, and carriers send cargo to Rotterdam and Gdańsk instead.

choices.label: Wait for the strike to end
choices.desc: Ships bound for Hamburg wait at anchor. No surcharges.

choices.label: Divert to Rotterdam
choices.desc: A surcharge of about €350 per container and a longer haul to the warehouse.

choices.label: Divert to Gdańsk
choices.desc: A surcharge of about €300 per container and 2–3 more days sailing across the Baltic.

outcomes.title: EU and China confirm the agreements
outcomes.body: Ministers confirm the easier licensing for rare earths and magnets. The Commission puts new trade defence measures on hold.

outcomes.title: Commission probes subsidies for Chinese car batteries and power electronics
outcomes.body: Brussels finds the progress insufficient and opens an anti-subsidy investigation into parts for electric cars. Provisional duties are possible in about four months.

events.title: Provisional duties on Chinese car batteries and power electronics
events.body: The Commission imposes provisional countervailing duties: 18% on power electronics and 15% on battery modules from China. Goods already in transit pay the duty on import. Competitors raise their prices.

events.title: Poland limits remote access to car electronics
events.body: Following the American rules on connected cars, the government limits remote access by makers from outside the EU to the electronics in cars on Polish roads. Some fleet customers now want power electronics and batteries made outside China.

events.title: Battery checks at the car inspection

outcomes.title: The inspection tests every electric car’s battery
outcomes.body: Germany adds a battery health check to the two-yearly car inspection. Owners bring in the cars that fail, and workshops order battery modules.

outcomes.title: The battery check is delayed
outcomes.body: A dispute over the test method delays the new check. Owners put off battery repairs until the rules are clear.

events.title: China closes lithium mines
events.body: Beijing closes small lithium mines in Jiangxi over their permits. Lithium and cell prices rise for a second month in a row, and battery modules in warehouses gain value.

events.title: Kazakhstan doubles capacity on the Chinese border
events.body: The expansion of the Dostyk and Altynkol stations finishes on schedule, raising capacity from 18 to 33 trains a day. Border queues disappear, and there is more space on the Caspian ferries.

events.title: Memory chips go on allocation
events.body: Memory makers put customers on quotas, and electronics companies fight for components. Makers of power electronics cut production.

events.title: Red Sea closed to shipping again
events.body: A security incident near Bab el-Mandeb closes the southern Red Sea to merchant ships. Carriers stop sailing through Suez and send their ships around Africa.

choices.label: Go around the Cape
choices.desc: Your ships that have not reached the strait sail around Africa: about 10–14 days longer and €300 per container.

choices.label: Sail in a protected convoy
choices.desc: The carrier keeps sailing in a protected convoy. €700 per container and a small risk of damage and delay.

choices.label: Wait in the Gulf of Aden
choices.desc: Ships wait for the strait to reopen. No surcharges, but nobody knows for how long.

events.title: Poland closes its border with Belarus
events.body: Citing security, the government closes the border crossings, including the rail crossing at Małaszewicze. Trains from China are stuck on the Belarusian side.

choices.label: Switch the autopilot to sea
choices.desc: New orders on the Belarus rail route will go via Suez.

choices.label: Stay with rail
choices.desc: Trains will wait for the border to reopen.

ml.why: Disruption risk is high: spreading suppliers and routes pays.
